name: Pattern 10: Pilot Small, Measure, Then Scale
title: Pattern 10: Pilot Small, Measure, Then Scale
answer: Pilot Small, Measure, Then Scale is the pattern for adopting any other AI idea in a school: try it with a few teachers for a set period, measure one thing that matters, and make a clear decision at the end to expand, adjust, or stop. It matters because realistic effects are small and promised time savings often fail to appear, so a small trial protects a district from spreading a mistake across every classroom.

crumbs.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere

sections.body: This pattern concerns how a school adopts any of the other nine patterns rather than what those patterns do. Instead of buying a tool for every classroom at once, the school tests it with a few teachers for a set period, tracks one measure that matters, and reaches a definite decision at the end. That decision can be to expand, to adjust, or to stop. Stopping counts as a success when the tool did not work, because it keeps the district from spreading a mistake. The problem it solves is adoption by default, where a purchase rolls out everywhere before anyone knows whether it helps.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: A good pilot is short and specific. It names two or three teachers, one measure such as minutes saved or a skill score, a starting baseline, and a date for the decision meeting. Figure 2.7 shows the shape of this, and Chapter 4 turns it into a full template. The text does not give separate grade band versions, so the same structure applies wherever the pilot runs. Every idea in this Volume should pass through a pilot like this before it reaches every classroom.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this as research and gives two reasons for caution. First, realistic effects are small, and short trials often show no learning gain even when students like the tool. In one randomized trial, students using AI scored higher on exercises but learned no more than students without it, and they preferred the tool that helped them least (Bassner et al., 2026). Second, promised time savings often fail to appear, and a review of automatic feedback found that nearly half the studies showed no reduction in instructor workload (Cavalcanti et al., 2021).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits sit in what a pilot can and cannot show. A short trial may show no learning gain even when students enjoy the tool, so liking a tool is not evidence that it teaches. Promised time savings may not materialise, so workload claims need their own measure. The decisions stay with people: the school chooses the two or three teachers, the single measure, the baseline, and the date, and people decide at the end whether to expand, adjust, or stop. Stopping is treated as a success when the tool did not work, which keeps the judgement with the school rather than with the product.
